title: The Absolute Dance: Hanover, the Sacred Mountain, and the Last Studio
register: national mythology, the canon is true

stops.name: Hanover, the house of the sewing-machine merchant
stops.campa: Karoline Sofie Marie Wiegmann is born 13 November 1886 in Hanover, into the solid house of a merchant who sells sewing machines and bicycles: the small precise engines of the bourgeois century. She is raised to its measures: the higher daughters' school from 1892, piano lessons, voice lessons, boarding schools in England and Switzerland, the grooming of a girl for a good marriage. Nothing in the ledgers of the firm foretells what sleeps in this child. But the body keeps its own ledger, and it is patient; it will wait more than twenty years to present the bill.
suggested_refs: Hugo Erfurth's early portrait photographs of Mary Wigman

stops.name: Amsterdam, the disciples of Dalcroze
stops.campa: After the failure of a first arranged engagement she is sent to an aunt in Amsterdam, a daughter in quarantine. There she sees students of Émile Jaques-Dalcroze demonstrate his rhythmic gymnastics: music made visible, walking and beating time in living bodies. It is the first crack of light under the door. She is eighteen, and the demonstration lodges in her like a splinter of the future: a name, Dalcroze, and a rumor that the body can be trained to speak. She returns to Hanover, to the parlor, to the second suitor already being arranged.
suggested_refs: Jaques-Dalcroze eurhythmics demonstration photographs, c. 1905

stops.name: Hanover, the Wiesenthal sisters and the speaking hands
stops.campa: The second engagement breaks, and the house turns cold: her parents see an old maid. Locked weeping in the guest room, she notices her own hands moving with her grief: the sorrow shaping itself in the fingers before any word. Soon after, Grete and Elsa Wiesenthal dance in Hanover, rebels out of Vienna against the corset of ballet, and it is their hands she cannot stop watching: hands that carry whole weathers of feeling. The two signs seal each other. At twenty-two, scandalously late, the merchant's daughter decides she will dance.
suggested_refs: Photographs of Grete Wiesenthal dancing the waltz, Vienna, c. 1908

stops.name: Hellerau, the Bildungsanstalt of Jaques-Dalcroze
stops.campa: At twenty-four, ancient for a beginner, she enrolls at the Bildungsanstalt für rhythmische Gymnastik in the garden city of Hellerau above Dresden, the model settlement where reformed furniture, reformed dress and reformed bodies are manufactured together. Under Dalcroze and the young Suzanne Perrottet she drills rhythm until it lives in the spine: bars walked, phrases breathed, music translated limb by limb. She is diligent and increasingly mutinous. The method makes the body a metronome of music, and something in her, unnamed yet, wants the body to be the music.
suggested_refs: The Festspielhaus Hellerau, temple of the rhythmic education

stops.name: Hellerau, the Festspielhaus: dance as the handmaid of music
stops.campa: In the white Festspielhaus, under Adolphe Appia's terraces and von Salzmann's walls of woven light, the festivals of Hellerau show Europe the new art of the trained body; Gluck's Orpheus moves through geometries of stairs and shadow, and pilgrims come from every capital. Marie Wiegmann is inside the machine and can feel its limit: here dance is forever the obedient daughter of the score, illustration and never utterance. Her body rebels against the servitude. She finishes her training carrying a heresy she cannot yet pronounce: that dance must stand alone, absolute.
suggested_refs: Appia's light-stage of the Festspielhaus Hellerau, Orpheus rehearsal photographs (1912-13)
sources: Manning, Ecstasy and the Demon: Feminism and Nationalism in the Dances of Mary Wigman

stops.name: Hellerau, Emil Nolde speaks the word 'Laban'
stops.campa: The painter Emil Nolde, prophet of the ecstatic in color, watches the dissatisfied pupil move and recognizes what her teachers cannot use. He gives her the word that turns the hinge of German dance: go to Rudolf von Laban, the Hungarian on the mountain above Ascona, who lets his students dance without music at all. Suzanne Perrottet is already leaving Dalcroze for the same fire. The canon marks Nolde's counsel as an annunciation: the expressionist painter dispatching the expressionist dancer to her master, art handing art the torch.
stops.quote: Und die Perrottet sagte, sie verläßt Dalcroze und geht zu einem Mann, der tolle Sachen macht, der ganz ohne Musik, seine Schüler ganz ohne Musik tanzen läßt.
stops.quote_source: Mary Wigman, late recollection of 1913, cited at gusto-graeser.info, 'Mary Wigman'
suggested_refs: Emil Nolde, Kerzentänzerinnen (Candle Dancers, 1912)

stops.name: Monte Verità, the climb to Laban
stops.campa: In the summer of 1913 she climbs the Mountain of Truth above Ascona, where vegetarians, anarchists, sun-worshippers and theosophists have made a republic of the reformed body, and enters Rudolf von Laban's School for Art. She comes for a summer course; she stays four years and leaves a different being. Laban watches her improvise and knows what has climbed to him: not a pupil but a force to be unbound. The atlas marks this meadow twice: the master with the doctrine, the dancer with the daimon, met above the lake.
suggested_refs: Photographs of Laban's dance farm on Monte Verità, 1913-14
laban.journey.json, 'Monte Verità: Mary Wigman climbs the hill' (Colegio Invisible atlas)

stops.name: Monte Verità, the daimon unbound
stops.campa: Barefoot on the meadow, in the sun-cult's loose robes, she dances for the first time without music: only breath, the drum, and the swing of her own weight. Laban makes her his assistant and his whetstone: he beats the gong and she hurls herself against space until space answers. What Hellerau forbade, the mountain commands. Here the vocabulary of Ausdruckstanz is smelted: tension and release, the body's fall and recovery, ecstasy given form. The merchant's daughter dissolves; out of the crucible steps Mary Wigman, first flame of the new German dance.
suggested_refs: Johann Adam Meisenbach's photographs of Laban's Monte Verità circle, 1914
sources: Mary Wigman, The Language of Dance (trans. Sorell, 1966)

stops.name: Munich, Palais Porcia: Lento and the first Witch Dance
stops.campa: On 11 February 1914, at the Museum in the Palais Porcia in Munich, asked by a colleague to fill out a program, she steps onto a stage as a soloist for the first time. In plain silk and bare feet, without one note of music, she dances Lento, and then Hexentanz, the Witch Dance, knees hammering the floor, fingers clawed, the demonic let loose in a drawing-room. The audience does not know it is watching a birth. The witch, once summoned, never leaves her; twelve years on she will return wearing a mask.
suggested_refs: Program of the solo evening at the Palais Porcia, Munich, 11 February 1914

stops.name: Monte Verità, the dance farm and the loaded pistol
stops.campa: The second summer on the mountain: Laban's little kingdom is a working dance farm where the pupils garden, cook, weave their costumes and dance, art and life composted together. Wigman and Perrottet deepen the experiments: swings, scales, the first sketches of a harmony of space modeled on crystals. It is the last summer of the old world. At Sarajevo, that same June, the pistol is being loaded; when it fires, the frontiers close around the mountain, and the school of the body must winter in neutral Zurich among the exiles.
suggested_refs: Laban's dancers photographed at harvest on the Monte Verità dance farm, summer 1914
sources: Green, Mountain of Truth: The Counterculture Begins, Ascona 1900-1920

stops.name: Zurich, the wartime school of dance, sound and word
stops.campa: Laban moves the work to Zurich, neutral hive of exiles, deserters, spies and prophets, and opens his school of dance, sound and word. Mary Wigman is his assistant: by day she drills the swings and scales into the pupils, by night the master hunts his alphabet of movement across graph paper while she tests each sign in her own joints. The school is poor, cold and incandescent: the laboratory where Ausdruckstanz is refined from mountain rite into discipline. Around them the city fills with every avant-garde the war has washed out of Europe.
suggested_refs: Photographs of Mary Wigman, Zurich years, 1915-18
sources: Mary Wigman, The Language of Dance (trans. Sorell, 1966)

stops.name: Zurich, the Galerie Dada on the Bahnhofstrasse
stops.campa: Two streets from the school, above the confectioner's on the Bahnhofstrasse, the Galerie Dada opens its soirées, and the two laboratories interpenetrate: Laban's dancers, Sophie Taeuber, Suzanne Perrottet, Käthe Wulff, cross over to dance in Marco Janco's abstract masks while Ball and Tzara detonate the word. Wigman drills the bodies that Dada borrows; the mask, the gong, the dance stripped of music and meaning down to pure force: the currency passes both ways. When her own witch later puts on a face of carved silver, Zurich is in it.
suggested_refs: Sophie Taeuber dancing in a Janco mask at the Galerie Dada, 1917 (photograph)
sources: Hugo Ball, Flight Out of Time (diary, 1917)

stops.name: Monte Verità, Sang an die Sonne: the sun sung down and up
stops.campa: At the close of the great congress on the mountain, Laban stages Sang an die Sonne across a whole night: the sun's descent danced at evening over the lake; at midnight, before Gusto Gräser's grotto, the demons of the night; at dawn the choir greets the rising sun as the promise that the war-winter of the world will end. Wigman dances on the meadow among the torches, priestess now, not pupil, in the movement choir consecrated as liturgy for a religion of the body, performed while the guns hold Europe.
suggested_refs: Sang an die Sonne, Monte Verità, August 1917, photographs of the torch-lit hymn

stops.name: The Walensee, the sanatorium and the Seven Dances written in fever
stops.campa: The war years call in their debt: her stepfather dead, her brother home from the front with a limb gone, a love ended, the partnership with Laban strained past bearing. She breaks, and is carried to a sanatorium above the Walensee in eastern Switzerland. Half a year she lies between the cliff and the grey lake, and there, unable to dance, she writes dance: Die sieben Tänze des Lebens, a dance-poem of desire, sorrow, the demon and death, composed entire in a notebook by a woman who cannot stand. The work waits three years for a body.
suggested_refs: Mary Wigman, Die sieben Tänze des Lebens: Tanzdichtung (published 1921)

stops.name: Berlin, the Philharmonie nearly empty
stops.campa: Risen from the sanatorium, thirty-two years old, she carries her strange gospel to Berlin and hires the Philharmonie. The hall is nearly empty; the capital, hungry and revolutionary, has no eyes yet for a woman dancing daemons without music. The failure is total and does not matter. She has seen what she is for, and an artist who has written dances from a sickbed is not to be refused by an empty room. She gathers the cycle, Ecstatic Dances, the temple pieces, and carries it from city to city like a contagion looking for its climate.
suggested_refs: Programs of Wigman's first solo tours, 1919

stops.name: Dresden, the hall of the merchants' guild says yes
stops.campa: On 7 November 1919, in the hall of the Dresden Kaufmannschaft, the climate is found. The city of the Brücke painters, primed by a decade of expressionism, recognizes at once what Berlin shrugged at: the evening is an extraordinary public triumph, and the merchants' guild-hall, of all rooms the temple of her father's class, is where the merchant's daughter is finally received as what she is. Dresden adopts her. Within a year she will plant her school here, and for two decades the city on the Elbe will be the Jerusalem of the absolute dance.
suggested_refs: Hugo Erfurth's Dresden portraits of Mary Wigman, c. 1919-20

segments.name: Dresden, the Temple of Absolute Dance

stops.name: Dresden, the school opens at the Postplatz
stops.campa: In 1920, with the devotion and the purse of her Swiss pupil Berthe Trümpy, she opens her own school in rooms of the Palasthotel Weber on the Postplatz. There is little money, less coal, and a doctrine: not steps but Gestaltung, the shaping of inner experience into visible form. Girls arrive from across the broken Reich and beyond it, hungry in every sense, and are put to the breath, the swing, the fall, the drum. The Wigman school will become the mother-house of an order that spreads to four cities and across an ocean.
suggested_refs: The Wigman school's first prospectus, Dresden 1920

stops.name: Dresden, the chamber dance group before the Philharmonic
stops.campa: On 14 January 1921 her first chamber dance group steps out with the Philharmonic in the Dresden concert hall; Wigman no longer a lone daimon but the center of a constellation: Berthe Trümpy, and soon the fierce young Gret Palucca, Yvonne Georgi, Hanya Holm, Harald Kreutzberg. Her credo is already law in the studio: ecstasy without form is convulsion, form without ecstasy is gymnastics; the dance is real only where the two are fused. The group tours, and Germany learns that the new dance is not one woman's seizure but a school, a language, an estate.
stops.quote: Without ecstasy no dance! Without form no dance!
stops.quote_source: Mary Wigman's credo, in The Mary Wigman Book, ed. Walter Sorell (1975)
suggested_refs: Charlotte Rudolph's photographs of the Wigman chamber dance group, Dresden, early 1920s
sources: The Mary Wigman Book, ed. Walter Sorell

stops.name: Frankfurt, Die sieben Tänze des Lebens made flesh
stops.campa: On 14 December 1921, at the Frankfurt opera house, the notebook from the Walensee sanatorium at last finds its bodies: Die sieben Tänze des Lebens is danced whole: the dance of longing, of love, of lust, of sorrow, the demon's dance, the dance of death, and through the veil of the last dance, life. What was written by a woman who could not stand is performed by the school she raised in the meantime. The canon reads the premiere as a resurrection performed in public: the illness composed, the composition now breathing.
suggested_refs: Mary Wigman, Die sieben Tänze des Lebens (Tanzdichtung, 1921)

stops.name: Dresden, the house on the Bautzner Strasse
stops.campa: The school outgrows hotel rooms and settles into its true temple, the villa grounds at Bautzner Strasse 107 above the Elbe: studios, garden, gong and drum, the hill-house where a generation of the century's dancers is formed. Palucca departs to found her own school, as daughters of this house do; Georgi, Kreutzberg, Holm carry the doctrine outward. Here Wigman teaches that dance is no entertainment of the theatres but a language older than them, and the pupils learn to speak it from the breath outward. The house still stands; dancers still keep it.
stops.quote: The dance is a living language which speaks of man — an artistic message soaring above the ground of reality in order to speak, on a higher level, in images and allegories of man's innermost emotions and need for communication.
stops.quote_source: Mary Wigman, The Language of Dance (trans. Walter Sorell, 1966), opening
suggested_refs: The Villa Wigman, Bautzner Strasse 107, Dresden, the school-house preserved
sources: Mary Wigman, The Language of Dance (1966)

stops.name: Dresden, Hexentanz II: the witch returns wearing a face
stops.campa: In 1926 the witch of the Palais Porcia comes back, and this time she has a face: a carved mask, remote and terrible, made after Wigman's own features and estranged from them. To rattles and percussion she dances seated and clawed, hammering the floor, the body shapeless in brocade, the mask smiling its fixed smile. The canon tells how the dance was given to her: late one night, hair wild over her nightgown, she catches herself in the mirror, and the mirror shows her the other one. The minutes of film that survive are the icon of Ausdruckstanz itself.
stops.quote: The image of one possessed, wild and dissolute, repelling and fascinating... there she was — the witch — the earth-bound creature with her unrestrained, naked instincts.
stops.quote_source: Mary Wigman, The Language of Dance (trans. Walter Sorell, 1966), on Hexentanz
suggested_refs: The surviving film fragment of Hexentanz II (1926/1930)
Charlotte Rudolph's photographs of Wigman in the witch mask
sources: Mary Wigman, The Language of Dance (1966)
Salem Witch Museum, 'Artists and the Witch Trials' (on Hexentanz II)

stops.name: Essen, the Second Dancers' Congress
stops.campa: At Essen the German dancers convene their second parliament, and the estate that Magdeburg founded now divides into its churches: Laban unveils his script, the kinetography that will bear his name; the ballet masters defend the theatres; and Wigman stands for the absolute dance: dance sovereign, serving neither opera nor notation nor decoration. The debates are doctrinal because the stakes are doctrinal: a new art is writing its constitution. She argues, as always, from the body outward, suspicious of every system that would fix in signs what lives only in the breath.
suggested_refs: Proceedings of the Second German Dancers' Congress, Essen 1928; first publication of Laban's Schrifttanz

stops.name: Dresden, Schwingende Landschaft: the swinging landscape
stops.campa: At the Dresden Schauspielhaus she dances the solo cycle Schwingende Landschaft, the swinging landscape, seven dances in which the daimon rests and the earth itself moves through her: summer's pastorale, the seraphic song, the wind's turning. After the witches and death-dances of the decade the canon reads this cycle as her psalter, the gentlest page in her book. She is at the summit: schools in Dresden, Berlin, Hamburg, Erfurt, Frankfurt; London conquered the year before; and across the water an impresario named Hurok is already counting the houses she will fill.
suggested_refs: Charlotte Rudolph's photograph series of Schwingende Landschaft (Pastorale, Seraphisches Lied), 1929

stops.name: Munich, Totenmal: the call to the dead of the war
stops.campa: At the Third Dancers' Congress in Munich, in a vast hall raised on the Theresienwiese, she and the poet Albert Talhoff stage Totenmal on 24 June 1930: a monument in word, light and movement to the dead of the Great War, speaking choirs against choirs of dancers, the women calling and the fallen answering, Wigman herself moving between the living and the dead as the veiled figure at the threshold. Sixteen hundred watch at each performance. The canon keeps Totenmal as the high mass of the movement choir, and the first tolling of the iron decade ahead.
suggested_refs: Photographs of Totenmal, Munich 1930, the speaking choir and the masked dead
sources: Dance Research Journal, 'From Totenmal to Trend: Wigman, Holm, and Theatricality in Modern Dance'

stops.name: New York, the Chanin Theatre: thunder on Broadway
stops.campa: Sol Hurok brings her across the ocean, and in the last days of December 1930 the curtain of the Chanin Theatre rises on a solitary German woman who dances to a gong and a drum. The house is sold out; the applause comes down like weather, a welcome she will carry to her deathbed. Depression America, which knows Denishawn's silks, has never seen this: space itself made adversary and partner. Martha Graham's generation is in the seats. Over three seasons she gives one hundred seventy performances across the continent, and modern dance becomes a two-shored art.
suggested_refs: Hurok tour programs and press for Mary Wigman's American debut season, 1930-31

stops.name: New York, the Wigman School of Hanya Holm
stops.campa: The mission plants its American house: the New York Wigman School opens under Hanya Holm, the quiet, exact apostle sent from the Dresden mother-house. Through her the doctrine of breath, swing and space enters the bloodstream of American dance: Holm will Americanize the school under her own name when the German name grows heavy, and her line runs on through Bessie Schönberg and Alwin Nikolais into everything after. The canon counts this storefront of studios among Wigman's most durable works: a school begotten of a school, begetting schools.
suggested_refs: Hanya Holm teaching at the New York Wigman School, photographs, early 1930s
sources: Dance Research Journal, 'From Totenmal to Trend'

stops.name: Dresden, the Gleichschaltung reaches the hill-house
stops.campa: The new masters of Germany take the culture into their fist, and the priestess of the absolute dance does not emigrate. She takes the local leadership of the dance section in the regime's teachers' league; she signs what is put before her; Jewish pupils and colleagues vanish from the rolls of the school and from the record of the art. The canon does not look away: she wagers that the German dance can ride the German state, and pays for the wager in every register: first with her conscience's company, later with the school itself.
suggested_refs: Wigman's essay collection Deutsche Tanzkunst (1935)

stops.name: Berlin, the German Dance Festival of the new state
stops.campa: At the German Dance Festival mounted under the Reich Culture Chamber in Berlin, Ausdruckstanz performs before the state that claims it as a national art. Wigman dances her women's dances; the halls are full; the ministries smile. It is the honeymoon of a marriage the canon already knows to be a devouring: the regime wants festival bodies and folk choirs, not daimons and witches, and the smile of official favor is the same fixed smile as the witch-mask's. Each season after this one, the freedom of the hill-house narrows by a degree.
suggested_refs: Programs of the Deutsche Tanzfestspiele, Berlin 1934

stops.name: Berlin, the Olympic Stadium: Totenklage before the hundred thousand
stops.campa: On the opening night of the Olympiad, in the festival play Olympische Jugend, Wigman leads eighty dancers in Totenklage, the lament for the dead, to Werner Egk's music, under the flame, before a hundred thousand in the Berlin stadium and the cameras of the world. It is the movement choir's greatest and last cathedral. She has refused to make the triumphal piece wanted of her; she gives the Games mourning instead, women grieving for the fallen at the feast of the nations that are three years from falling on each other. The regime does not forgive the gift.
suggested_refs: Film of Olympische Jugend, Olympic Stadium, 1 August 1936, the Totenklage choir

stops.name: Dresden, the long disfavor
stops.campa: After the Games the cold sets in. The subsidies thin, the invitations lapse, the ministry's word for her art hardens toward the vocabulary it uses for the condemned painters. She dances the Herbstliche Tänze, the autumnal dances, a title the canon hears as plain speech, and holds the school together year by year as the war comes and takes the students, the coal, the light. Her companion of the Nazi years, an industrialist bound to the armaments state, is pressed apart from her. The regime that embraced the German dance is strangling it with the same arms.
suggested_refs: Charlotte Rudolph's photographs of the Herbstliche Tänze cycle, 1937

stops.name: Dresden, the school sold, the farewell danced
stops.campa: On 1 April 1942 the hill-house passes from her hands: the Wigman school is sold and swallowed as a department of the Dresden conservatory. That year, at the Komödienhaus, the fifty-five-year-old dances her last solo evening and names it what it is: Abschied und Dank, farewell and thanks. The woman who entered as the witch goes out as the guest thanking the house. Twenty-two years of the Dresden temple end in an inventory and a bow. She leaves for Leipzig, a teacher without a school, carrying the language in her body like contraband.
suggested_refs: Program of Abschied und Dank, Wigman's final solo evening, Dresden 1942

stops.name: Leipzig, teaching under the bombs
stops.campa: In Leipzig, where her sister Elisabeth had kept a school before her, she teaches dance at the Musikhochschule while the air war dismantles the city around the lessons. The studio work goes on between alarms: breath, swing, fall, recovery; the curriculum now indistinguishable from instructions for surviving. The pupils are girls of the catastrophe; she is their proof that the art has outlived one German collapse already and intends to outlive another. In the nights she writes, and waits, one more winter resident in the long sanatorium that Germany has become.
suggested_refs: The Hochschule für Musik, Grassistrasse 8, Leipzig, Wigman's wartime teaching rooms

stops.name: Leipzig, the night Dresden burns
stops.campa: On the night of 13 February 1945 the firestorm takes Dresden. Word and, the tradition says, the glow on the horizon reaches Leipzig, and Wigman keeps vigil for the city of her ascension: the guild-hall of the first triumph, the Postplatz rooms, the theatres, the streets her pupils crossed for twenty years, burning in one night. The hill-house on the Bautzner Strasse survives above the ruin like a relic. The canon sets this among her death-dances: Totenmal was danced for the last war's dead, and the new dead now outnumber every choir.
suggested_refs: The ruins of Dresden, February 1945; the surviving Villa Wigman above the Elbe

stops.name: Leipzig, professor at sixty
stops.campa: The war ends and she is still standing, sixty years old in the Soviet zone, and she builds again: at the reopened Hochschule she heads the dance department and installs a four-semester training; on her sixtieth birthday the new order names her professor. In the spring she petitions for a central academy of dance for the whole of Germany: the old dream of the dancers' congresses, filed now with commissars. She choreographs, teaches, examines: the daimon in a professor's chair, conducting the language of dance through the rubble semester by semester.
suggested_refs: Wigman's memorandum for a central dance academy, Leipzig, April 1947

stops.name: Leipzig, Orpheus again: the ring closes on Hellerau
stops.campa: For the Leipzig opera she choreographs Gluck's Orpheus und Eurydike: the very work through which, as a mutinous pupil at Hellerau thirty-five years before, she first felt dance chafing in the service of music. Now the servant returns as master of the rite: her Orpheus descends among the shades in a Germany that is itself an underworld, and the plea to lead the beloved dead back into the light is understood by every soul in the house. The canon loves such rings; it marks this one and counts the years, 1912 to 1947, like beads.
suggested_refs: Production records of Orpheus und Eurydike, Leipzig opera, 1947

stops.name: Berlin-Dahlem, the flight west and the third founding
stops.campa: In the spring of 1949 the state nationalizes her Leipzig work out from under her, and on the fourth of July she crosses to West Berlin, sixty-two years old, founding for the third time. In a villa on the Rheinbabenallee in Dahlem she opens the Mary Wigman-Studio with Marianne Vogelsang: bare floor, drum, gong, the whole apparatus of the language reassembled once more. To this room come the postwar pilgrims from every continent; among the last of them, a quiet Japanese student named Kazuo Ohno's generation carries the seed onward into butoh's dark.
suggested_refs: The Mary Wigman-Studio, Rheinbabenallee 35, Berlin-Dahlem, photographs of classes, 1950s

stops.name: Mannheim, Saul and the Carmina: the choirs return
stops.campa: The opera houses of the Federal Republic call her back to the large form: at the Mannheim Nationaltheater she stages Handel's Saul, then Orff's Catulli Carmina and Carmina Burana: the medieval wheel of fortune turned by a woman whom fortune's wheel has carried up, down, and up again. The movement choir, born on a Swiss mountain and buried in the Olympic stadium, is resurrected in oratorio. The same year the Akademie der Künste elects her: the republic, needing ancestors it can honor, finds one still alive and still working.
suggested_refs: Production photographs of Wigman's Carmina Burana, Nationaltheater Mannheim, 1955

stops.name: Berlin, Le Sacre du printemps: the last spring sacrifice
stops.campa: On 24 September 1957, for the Berlin Festwochen at the Städtische Oper, the seventy-year-old stages her final great work: Stravinsky's Sacre du printemps with forty-five dancers, Dore Hoyer, the last flame of Ausdruckstanz, as the Chosen One. The woman who began by dancing alone in silence ends by commanding the century's loudest score, and the theme is the one she has served all her life: the single body given to the earth so that the tribe's year may turn. The ovation is long. She lays down the choreographer's rod with the sacrifice completed.
suggested_refs: Photographs of Wigman's Sacre du printemps, Berlin 1957, Dore Hoyer as the Chosen One; reconstructed 2013 (Tanzfonds Erbe)
sources: tanzfonds.de, 'Le Sacre du Printemps by Mary Wigman'

stops.name: Berlin-Dahlem, the studio closes, the book remains
stops.campa: In 1967, past eighty, she closes the Dahlem studio, the last room of the last school, and the teaching passes wholly into the written word and the visits of disciples. Her book Die Sprache des Tanzes has gone out into English as The Language of Dance; in its pages the witch, the mountain, the masks and the choirs are laid up like vestments in a sacristy. She receives the honors of two republics and the pilgrimages of three generations, and insists to the end that the source is not doctrine but the lived, breathing body.
stops.quote: Strong and convincing art has never arisen from theories.
stops.quote_source: Mary Wigman, The Language of Dance (trans. Walter Sorell, 1966)
suggested_refs: Mary Wigman, Die Sprache des Tanzes (1963) / The Language of Dance (1966)
sources: Mary Wigman, The Language of Dance (1966)

stops.name: Berlin, the death of the dancer
stops.campa: On 18 September 1973, in Berlin, Mary Wigman dies in her eighty-seventh year. The obituaries of two Germanys and two continents say the same thing in their different tongues: that she found dance a decoration and left it a language; that she stood alone on bare stages without music and made space itself visible; that the modern dance of Europe and much of America descends from her breath. The daimon that came to a weeping girl in a locked room in Hanover has used the body up completely, which is what bodies are for.

stops.name: Essen, the urn in the family grave at the Ostfriedhof
stops.campa: On 14 November 1973, the day after what would have been her eighty-seventh birthday, her urn is laid in the Wiegmann family grave at the Ostfriedhof in Essen, and Gret Palucca, first and fiercest of the daughters, speaks the funeral oration. The circle the canon draws is exact: the merchant's daughter returns to the family plot, but the stone set for her bears the other name, the stage name, the name of the work. Marie Wiegmann lies with her family; Mary Wigman belongs to the language she left in the bodies of the living.
